new_statements.quote: Sumtu syllables are very frequently preceded by an unstressed syllable, often as part of the system of prefixational morphology. These syllables are described here as minor syllables because they may only contain a short, non-contrastive epenthetic schwa [ə̆] which is not transcribed, even though it necessarily bears a tone. [p.99] ... Like many languages in the mainland South-East Asian linguistic area, Sumtu has many words iambic in form, as described in 2.4. Unrestricted major syllables, which may have the form of any permitted syllable in the language, may be preceded by a restricted half-syllable comprising a single initial consonant (most commonly ʔ) and a short epenthetic schwa [ə̆] [p.115]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sumtu is a tone language: every syllable, major or minor, carries lexical or assigned high or low tone. The only stress statement is structural: words are often sesquisyllabic/iambic, a reduced minor syllable (C + short epenthetic schwa, optionally + m/n) that is explicitly 'unstressed' preceding the full major syllable, which is the prominent syllable and the one the foot's single lexical tone aligns with; the minor syllable receives the polar-opposite tone. Prominence thus falls on the final (major) syllable of the iambic foot; nothing is said about stress placement in words of two full syllables or in longer compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Minor syllables may be lexical (sesquisyllabic nouns) or prefixes (pronominal, transitive -m, non-singular -n); a non-syllabic prefix m- before a stop is not a minor syllable (p.100, ex. 1a, 1e). Tone behaviour (polarity, OCP, dual tone flip) is the paper's focus and has its own complications.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic lexemes and prefix+stem words) in a single speaker's Myebon dialect, elicited from a 68-lesson reader read aloud; 'stressed' on p.117 ('Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus') is phrase-level emphasis, not word stress. Author states the segmental phonology is outside the paper's scope.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Myebon-township dialect of Sumtu Chin [csv] sumt1234 as spoken by one elderly speaker (Dong Ling, author of the 2008 Sumtu Reader); Watkins notes tones and vowels differ significantly between Sumtu dialects. Glottolog's cited title is the SOAS WPL 16 working-paper version ('A first look at tone...'); the file held is the peer-reviewed LTBA 36(2) version ('A first account of tone...'), same author and year. Sumtu is closely related to but distinct from Laitu Chin [clj] lait1239 and Songlai Chin [csj] song1313 (both undescribed).
